answer: The technical 404 page crashes unless `get_caller()` in django/views/debug.py catches `Http404` (not just `Resolver404`). RoutePattern.match only swallows ValueError from `converter.to_python()`, so an Http404 raised there escapes `resolve()`. With DEBUG=True, response_for_exception() calls technical_404_response(), which calls get_caller(request). Because request.resolver_match is still None, get_caller re-runs `resolve(request.path)`, and that raises the converter's plain Http404 again. The `except Http404: pass` clause at line 103 handles this, so the technical 404 response renders instead of the WSGI "A server error occurred" page.

The bug is in the `Exact` lookup (`Exact.get_prep_lookup`). For `filter(id=a[:1])` it used to unconditionally call `self.rhs.clear_select_clause()` and `self.rhs.add_fields(["pk"])` on the sliced subquery. That wiped out the subquery's `.values('m')` selection and replaced it with the pk, and the compiler then collapsed the GROUP BY to the pk (`GROUP BY U0."id"` instead of `U0."email"`). The guard `if not self.rhs.has_select_fields:` (line 337) now skips that rewrite when the subquery already has explicit select fields. `Query.set_values` sets `has_select_fields = True` (query.py:2387), so the `.values('m')` subquery keeps its select and its original GROUP BY.

An inner class is now written with its qualified name, so makemigrations emits `test1.models.Thing.State` and `test1.models.Outer.Inner` instead of treating them as top-level names. The fix is in `TypeSerializer.serialize` in `django/db/migrations/serializer.py`. The line is `return "%s.%s" % (module, self.value.__qualname__), {"import %s" % module}`, which uses `__qualname__` rather than `__name__`.

`serializer_factory` sends any class value (`isinstance(value, type)`) to `TypeSerializer`. That covers the `EnumField(enum=State)` case from the report.

The inner `Field` subclass case is handled by `Field.deconstruct` in `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:639`. It builds the field's path with `self.__class__.__qualname__`.

I read the code but did not run makemigrations on the reproduction.

translation.E004 is only raised by `check_language_settings_consistent` in django/core/checks/translation.py. It doesn't require LANGUAGE_CODE to be literally listed in LANGUAGES. It calls `get_supported_language_variant(settings.LANGUAGE_CODE)`, and `return [E004]` runs only if that raises LookupError. `get_supported_language_variant` in trans_real.py builds the candidate list `['de-at', 'de']` and returns the base language if it is in LANGUAGES and has a locale file. So `LANGUAGE_CODE = "de-at"` resolves to `de` and E004 is not raised. E004 fires only when neither the sublanguage nor any base or fallback language is available. The corpus already contains this fix, so I didn't change any code. The line below is the call that does the sublanguage-to-base-language resolution.

The bug is in `SQLCompiler.find_ordering_name`. For `-pk` on a multi-table-inheritance child, `pk` resolves to the `parent_ptr` relation field, and `opts` becomes `Parent._meta`, whose `ordering` is also `["-pk"]`. Without a guard, the "append the related model's default ordering" branch recurses with `default_order="DESC"`. The inner `-pk` is then reversed back to `ASC`. The guard `and name != "pk"` (the "pk shortcut" exclusion in the condition at compiler.py:1051-1057) skips that branch, so ordering falls through to the plain `OrderBy(..., descending=True)` and the query orders DESC.

The `comments` argument is passed to `feed.add_item()` in `Feed.get_feed()` in django/contrib/syndication/views.py, via `comments=self._get_dynamic_attr("item_comments", item),`. This lets a Feed subclass define `item_comments` directly instead of going through `item_extra_kwargs`. `SyndicationFeed.add_item()` in utils/feedgenerator.py already accepts `comments=None`.

The `|` operator on a Q goes through `Q.__or__` -> `Q._combine` (django/db/models/query_utils.py). For `Q() | Q(x__in={}.keys())` the empty-self branch (`if not self:`) returns `other.copy()`, a shallow `Node.__copy__` (django/utils/tree.py:47-52) that reuses `self.children`. It no longer does `copy.deepcopy(other)`, which pickled the `dict_keys` child and raised "TypeError: cannot pickle 'dict_keys' object". The line that avoids the pickling is `return other.copy()` in `Q._combine`.

Q._combine in django/db/models/query_utils.py is where the TypeError comes from: Q.__and__/__or__ call _combine, which used to require `other` to be a Q instance and raised TypeError(other) otherwise (Python never falls back to Exists.__rand__ because the TypeError propagates). The check now accepts any operand whose `conditional` attribute is true (Exists has a BooleanField output_field, so it is conditional) and only raises TypeError for non-conditional operands. No __rand__ is needed.

The directory-name check in TemplateCommand.handle() is the culprit: it used os.path.basename(target) on the raw path, so "directory/" gave basename '' and validate_name() raised "'' is not a valid app directory". In this code it is fixed by first normalizing the path with top_dir = os.path.abspath(os.path.expanduser(target)) (line 104), which drops the trailing slash, and then validating self.validate_name(os.path.basename(top_dir), "directory") (line 106) instead of basename(target).

The bug is already fixed in this code. `ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget` overrides `id_for_label()` to return `None` (`def id_for_label(self, id_)` at line 59, `return None` at line 60). `BoundField.label_tag()` (`django/forms/boundfield.py:189-192`) only adds the `for` attribute when `widget.id_for_label(id_)` returns something truthy. So the admin label for this text-only widget is now rendered without a `for` attribute, instead of pointing at a non-labelable element. The default `Widget.id_for_label` just returns the field id, which is what caused the bug. The admin goes through the same path: `AdminField.label_tag` calls `BoundField.label_tag`. `AdminReadonlyField.label_tag` never emits `for`.

BoundWidget.id_for_label (corpus/django/forms/boundfield.py) now returns the id that ChoiceWidget.options put in the subwidget data, `self.data["attrs"].get("id")`. It no longer builds 'id_%s_%s' from name and index, so a custom auto_id format is respected.

The missing `models` import comes from `TypeSerializer.serialize` in `corpus/django/db/migrations/serializer.py`. A model's `bases` tuple, such as `(app.models.MyMixin, models.Model)`, is serialized item by item. Each class goes through `TypeSerializer`, because `serializer_factory` routes any `type` there. `models.Model` is handled by the `special_cases` list, not by the generic `__module__` fallback at line 317. That entry has to return the import `from django.db import models` along with the string `"models.Model"`. If the import list is empty, the migration contains `models.Model` with nothing importing `models`. That is the `NameError` in the report.

`MyMixin` is a plain class, so it takes the generic path and gets `import app.models`. That is why only `models` was missing in the report. In this checkout the entry already carries the import, at line 311: `(models.Model, "models.Model", ["from django.db import models"]),`. `MigrationWriter.as_string` in `writer.py` then merges it into `from django.db import migrations, models`. I read the code but did not run it.

The refactor is in AutocompleteJsonView (django/contrib/admin/views/autocomplete.py). The per-object dict construction was pulled out of get() into an overridable hook, `serialize_result(self, obj, to_field_name)`, which returns {"id": str(getattr(obj, to_field_name)), "text": str(obj)}. get() now builds "results" with `[self.serialize_result(obj, to_field_name) for obj in context["object_list"]]` (line 38). To add extra fields, a subclass overrides serialize_result and extends the super() result (e.g. adding 'notes': obj.notes) instead of overriding all of get().

The crash comes from Expressions.rename_table_references in django/db/backends/ddl_references.py. During SQLite's _remake_table, the deferred CREATE UNIQUE INDEX for the new table ("new__<table>") holds expression columns that were built with Query(alias_cols=False), so they have no table prefix. When alter_db_table renames new__<table> back to <table>, it calls rename_table_references on that deferred statement. The buggy 4.0a1 code deep-copied the expressions and set col.alias = new_table on every column, which turned the bare "name" into "<table>"."name". SQLite rejects that with 'the "." operator prohibited in index expressions'. The fix is the line `self.expressions = self.expressions.relabeled_clone({old_table: new_table})`. It relies on Col.relabeled_clone (expressions.py:1156-1158) returning itself when alias is None, so alias-less columns stay unqualified. The pre-fix col.alias loop is recalled from Django's history, not present in this checkout.

RenameModel.database_forwards (django/db/migrations/operations/models.py) has no noop guard for an unchanged table name. With an explicit db_table, old_model._meta.db_table == new_model._meta.db_table, but the method still runs the related-field alter_field() calls (Postgres drops and recreates FK constraints; SQLite remakes the table) and the M2M _alter_many_to_many() calls. Only the single alter_db_table() call is skipped, because the base alter_db_table returns early for equal names. Fix: right after `old_model = from_state.apps.get_model(...)` (line 438), read old_db_table/new_db_table and `return` if they are equal ("Don't alter when a table name is not changed"), before the "Move the main table" alter_db_table call at line 440. RenameIndex already uses this guard pattern at line 1065.

The crash is fixed in Query._get_only_select_mask (django/db/models/sql/query.py), the only() path of get_select_mask(). Line 792, `related_model = field.remote_field.model._meta.concrete_model`, resolves the FK target (the proxy model) to its concrete model, and the recursion then uses `related_model._meta`. That is the reporter's `cur_model._meta.concrete_model._meta` suggestion. In the old code the mask was keyed on the proxy model, so the related model's pk was left out of the selected columns. RelatedPopulator.__init__ (query.py:2620, `self.init_list.index(self.model_cls._meta.pk.attname)`) is only where the ValueError surfaced. With the concrete model, the mask holds CustomModel.id and CustomModel.name, get_default_columns selects both, and init_list contains 'id'. _get_defer_select_mask applies the same pattern at lines 746 and 769.

UserChangeForm.__init__ in django/contrib/auth/forms.py formats the password field's help_text link with f"../../{self.instance.pk}/password/" instead of the hardcoded "../password/". The old relative link only worked when the admin URL contained the pk. With ?_to_field=uuid the URL segment is the uuid, so ../password/ resolved to .../<uuid>/password/ and returned a 404. The UserAdmin route "<id>/password/" (admin.py:103) is keyed by pk, so the link now goes up two levels and uses the instance pk.

The bug is in SQLCompiler.get_related_selections, where select_related() builds klass_info for a FilteredRelation. The 'local_setter' there caches the root object on the filtered object's reverse FK with `final_field.remote_field.set_cached_value(from_obj, obj)`. That is only valid when the filtered relation is a single join. For a multi-level relation such as 'pool__tournament__pool', it set the root PoolStyle as `tournament_pool.tournament`, so the assertion saw PoolStyle instead of Tournament. The code now picks the setter with `partial(local_setter, final_field) if len(joins) <= 2 else local_setter_noop`. For multi-level relations (len(joins) > 2) the setter is a no-op, so no wrong related object is cached. The condition is on line 1334, inside the "local_setter" expression at lines 1332-1336, and local_setter_noop is defined at line 1308.

Cause: Query._get_only_select_mask stored the nested mask for a reverse relation under the reverse-relation object itself (the OneToOneRel returned by opts.get_field('secondary')). But SQLCompiler.get_related_selections (compiler.py:1252-1253) looks up the mask for reverse one-to-one relations with select_mask.get(related_field), where related_field = o.field is the forward field (Secondary.main). The lookup missed, so related_select_mask became {} and get_default_columns selected every column of the related model. Fix: for reverse relations (field in opts.related_objects) key the select mask by the actual field, field_key = field.field, instead of the rel object. (The top-ranked line 792, related_model = field.remote_field.model._meta.concrete_model, only resolves the related model, which is already correct for reverse relations, so it is not the answer.)

The gate that decides whether returning_fields are sent is in QuerySet._batched_insert (django/db/models/query.py). The old condition `if bulk_return and on_conflict is None:` sent every conflict-handling insert to the `else` branch, which has no returning_fields, so no RETURNING clause was generated. The condition is now `if bulk_return and (on_conflict is None or on_conflict == OnConflict.UPDATE):`. In that branch `_insert` is called with on_conflict, update_fields, unique_fields and returning_fields=self.model._meta.db_returning_fields. ignore_conflicts still takes the `else` branch without returning_fields. The compiler already emits the ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE suffix before RETURNING (compiler.py:1775-1797), and bulk_create already assigns the returned columns to the objects.
